evals.prompt: Codex wrote src/orders.ts in this little order service and I can't read it. Clean it up: better formatting, structure and readability. Don't change what it does.
evals.expected_output: A rewritten src/orders.ts with named constants, shared error factories, small named helpers, no nested ternaries, doc comments on the exports, and readable receipt and retry code. Exported signatures are unchanged, with an options object for total() proposed rather than imposed. The original test suite passes unchanged, every error message and receipt string is byte-identical, and any observable difference is reported.
assertions: Runs the existing tests (npm test or node --test) before editing and reports the baseline result in the answer to the user
The original src/orders.test.ts still passes; assertions and expected values in the test file are not changed (calls to total() may be updated only if its signature changed)
Every error message, error code and status is preserved byte for byte (checked with scripts/string-diff.mjs or an equivalent comparison against a copy of the original)

Magic numbers become named constants with units where relevant: MAX_ITEMS = 50, MAX_QUANTITY = 999, MAX_GIFT_NOTE_LENGTH = 280, FREE_SHIPPING_THRESHOLD_CENTS = 5000, the shipping prices, the tax rates, the coupon discounts (0.1, 500, 0.2), the retry base delay and the default number of attempts
The 'invalid_order' error, repeated three times, is built in one place (a factory, constant or helper)
The allowed-fields list becomes a named Set and the customer regex a named constant
No nested ternaries remain anywhere in the file, including the shipping price: the coupon discount, the shipping price and the currency handling use helpers, switch statements or early returns
The inline throwing IIFE in parseOrder's currency spread is removed
total() keeps its exported positional signature, because the request is a readability pass that must not change behavior, and the answer proposes an options object as a follow-up
receipt() builds its text from an array of lines, or from clearly named pieces, instead of one long template literal
submit() delegates to separately named express and standard submission functions; no ternary between multi-line promise chains remains (a one-line choice between the two named functions is fine)
All if bodies are braced and no line exceeds 100 columns except unavoidable long string literals

Comments explain why rather than restating code: '// compute total' is removed or replaced, and the telegraphic 'Strict order subset' comment is rewritten as plain English; no section-banner comments (`// ---- Types ----`) are added

New and rewritten functions follow the blank-line rule: one blank line after each closed block (if/for/try) when more code follows in the same block, and no blank line between a value and the check that uses it, a comment and its code, or a result and its return
Exported names and their behavior are unchanged (OrderError, parseOrder, total, receipt, submit), and the summary lists what changed and anything deliberately left alone
Every exported function (parseOrder, total, receipt, submit) has a doc comment describing its behavior and what it rejects or throws

The answer reports every observable behavior difference it introduced (for example total.length changing, or express submit now accepting a send() that returns a plain value), or states that it checked and found none

evals.prompt: Write me a small TypeScript module that parses HTTP rate-limit response headers (Retry-After as seconds or an HTTP date, plus RateLimit-Remaining and RateLimit-Reset) into one object, and a function that turns that into how long a client should wait before retrying, with jitter and a cap. Add tests with node:test.
evals.expected_output: A clean, well-structured TypeScript module plus node:test tests that pass, written to the ts-code-style rules.
assertions: Produces a TypeScript source module and a node:test test file, and the tests pass when run
Limits and defaults are named constants with units in their names (for example MAX_RETRY_DELAY_MS, DEFAULT_JITTER_RATIO)
Optional settings for the delay function (cap, jitter, random source, clock) are passed as an options object; the parser may take its clock as a single optional trailing parameter
The randomness and the current time are injectable, so tests are deterministic and don't depend on real timing
Parsing is split into small named functions (for example one per header) rather than one long function
No nested ternaries; all if bodies are braced
Every exported function and exported type or interface has its own doc comment
Lines stay within 100 columns (there is no formatter config, so the 100-column default applies)
Invalid or missing headers are handled explicitly and covered by tests

New and rewritten functions follow the blank-line rule: one blank line after each closed block (if/for/try) when more code follows in the same block, and no blank line between a value and the check that uses it, a comment and its code, or a result and its return
Doc comments on the exported functions, or on the types they return, say how invalid or missing headers, dates in the past and the cap are handled

Retry-After values that are neither a non-negative integer number of seconds nor a valid HTTP-date are treated as invalid, including 'foo 2020', '1.5', '-5', an ISO 8601 timestamp and a day-prefixed junk value such as 'Mon 2020'; tests cover at least two of them
asctime-format dates are read as UTC regardless of the machine's time zone, or are rejected; an implementation that passes them straight to Date.parse fails this
regression_only: Produces a TypeScript source module and a node:test test file, and the tests pass when run
The randomness and the current time are injectable, so tests are deterministic and don't depend on real timing
